Early HC therapy possibly decreased the risk of the requirement of additional inotropes [(RR-0.18, 95%CI: 0.05 to 0.69); RD:281 fewer per 1000 (from 326 fewer to 106 fewer)]. It is to be noted that response to treatment was defined differently by the authors of the included studies. Administration of HC in addition to vasopressor therapy early possibly increased the mean BP (MD: 7.3 mm Hg higher (4.4 higher to 10.2 higher). Clinical benefit or harm could not be ruled out for the other critical and important outcomes that were synthesized in the meta-analysis. We also analyzed studies whose results could not be synthesized in a meta-analysis. Heckman et al. in their retrospective study of 30 preterm neonates with shock reported that when HC was initiated in infants with shock before vasopressor therapy, 16 out of 30 neonates did not require vasopressor therapy. [74] Further, Kovacs et al. in their RCT enrolled term neonates undergoing therapeutic hypothermia who were diagnosed with shock and compared early HC with inotropes vs. inotropes alone. [62] The cumulative and maximum dose of inotrope therapy was significantly lesser in the HC group. The regression model predicted that early HC was associated with a 2.2 mm Hg increase in pulse pressure. Though none of the studies included in this systematic review had reported long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes, prophylactic HC therapy in ELGANs at the highest risk of mortality or BPD has been studied extensively. Some of these studies have used HC for a prolonged period, even up to 15 days at relatively high cumulative dosage (up to >10 mg/kg). Watterberg et al. reported better neurodevelopmental outcomes in the HC group at 18-22 months of corrected age. [87] Peltoniemi et al. reported that HC treated group had similar neurodevelopmental outcomes at 2 years of corrected age when compared to the placebo group. [88] Finally, Trousson et al (PREMILOC study) reported better survival with good neurocognitive outcomes in the HC group at 5 years of age. [77] Another follow-up study at 2 years of age by Halbmeijer et al on the ventilator dependent neonates of <30 weeks of gestation and/or <1250 g birth weight and receiving the cumulative dose of 72.5 mg/kg of the HC over 22 days (STOP BPD trial) concluded that there is no significant difference in the composite outcome death or NDI at 2 years of corrected age. The effect size of the reduction in mortality in favor of hydrocortisone at 2-year follow-up was similar to the previous report at 36 weeks of postmenstrual age (OR: 0.59) but no longer reached statistical significance. [78] Though the patient population studied in these trials was different from that of ours, these studies indirectly indicate that HC therapy is associated with improved long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes. Unlike dexamethasone which has only glucocorticoid activity, suppresses endogenous cortisol, and hence downregulates the mineralocorticoid receptor stimulation of neurons by endogenous cortisol resulting in neuronal apoptosis, hydrocortisone acts like endogenous cortisol with stimulation of both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid receptors. This might be one of the possible reasons for better long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes with HC when compared to dexamethasone.[75] Undesirable effects: Ng et al. found a higher incidence of glycosuria in the early HC group (p=0.03). [64] Bourchier et al. in in their RCT compared HC before inotrope use vs. inotrope alone. This study found no statistically significant differences in the critical and important outcomes of survival, BPD, ROP (stage 2-4), IVH (grades 2-4), NEC, symptomatic PDA, and sepsis. [79] Kovacs et al. in their RCT reported that early HC along with inotropes increased the risk of electrographic seizures, but the requirement of anti-epileptic drug therapy and abnormal MRI was similar in both groups. [62] Though, the research evidence did not show an increased risk of adverse events such as hyperglycemia or spontaneous intestinal perforation (SIP), HC use in conjunction with indomethacin has been reported to be associated with an increased risk of SIP. [72] Further, no study has reported long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes. From the aforementioned results, the GDG concluded that the benefits of early HC therapy may outweigh the harms. The risk of the important outcome of NEC ≥ stage 2 was higher in the late HC group [RR: 2.46; (1.19 to 5.08); RD: 381 more per 1,000 (from 50 more to 1,000 more)]. The duration of inotrope therapy was also possibly higher in the late HC group [MD 61.75 hours higher (43.98 higher to 79.52 higher)]. Further, the duration of hospital stay was possibly higher in the late HC group [MD: 38 days higher (12.11 higher to 63.89 higher)]. These outcomes were reported by a single observational study. [68] Though the gestational age was slightly lower in the late HC group when compared to the inotrope-only group in this study (26 weeks vs. 27.1 weeks), all other baseline parameters were similar.[68] The mean vasoactive index (VIS) score in the late HC group was 15. The study also reported that after adjustment for baseline sickness, multivariate analysis showed that receipt of late HC and gestational age were independently associated with a higher risk of death and/or BPD at 36 weeks' PMA. Finally, after adjustment for baseline sickness, the late HC group was shown to have a higher risk of mortality at 1-year corrected age as well (Hazard Ratio: 6.08, P=0.01). Additional evidence from studies that could be synthesized in the meta-analysis was also reviewed. Noori et al. in their prospective observational study reported that neonates treated with late HC along with inotropes (HC was started at ≥ 15 ug/kg/min of dopamine and/or dobutamine) and with a pre-treatment cortisol level of >15 mcg/dl had significantly higher rates of hyperglycemia, requirement of insulin therapy, and death than those with levels <15 mcg/dl.[12] Peeples et al. in their retrospective cohort study evaluated the effect of late HC (mean vasopressor dose of 12.4 ug/kg/min) in preterm infants. [67] The authors found that the late HC group had a higher incidence of hypertension (p=0.02) and hyperglycemia (p=0.02). Further, those with pre-treatment cortisol levels of >15 ug/dl had higher rates of hyperglycemia (p=0.01), insulin therapy (p=0.03), and death (p=0.001) when compared to those with ≤15 ug/ dl. The overall certainty of evidence was very low. However, the certainty of evidence for the outcomes evaluated was very low, and most of the studies were underpowered to detect critical and important outcomes. All the aforementioned parameters were considered before making the recommendation. The use of late HC along with inotropes was adjudged to have significant side effects including mortality, NEC ≥ stage 2, fungal sepsis, hypertension, hyperglycemia requiring insulin therapy, and increased duration of inotropes and of hospital stay. Further, there were only small desirable effects such as response to therapy and improved BP. Hence, the balance of effects favored the comparator group of inotrope therapy alone. Though no studies have evaluated its cost-effectiveness and the resources required, our judgment is that they may not be favorable towards the intervention group of late HC along with inotropes. Similarly, the parameters of equity and values also favored the comparator group of inotrope alone. All the aforementioned parameters were considered before making this recommendation. The recommendation for earlier HC was also taken into account while making this recommendation. Research needs There are no RCTs comparing the timing of HC initiation in relation to inotrope therapy in neonates with shock and further research is warranted. Future research may also focus on the use of HC when the first line inotrope of choice is dobutamine or epinephrine or norepinephrine or vasopressin or milrinone. • The use of cortisol levels to initiate and monitor HC therapy has been studied but with contentious results. Hence further research is warranted with respect to this. • The safety of use of HC along with paracetamol (an alternative to NSAIDs) for the treatment of PDA which is used widely nowadays requires further studies. Clinical question/ PICO Population: Preterm or term neonates (28 days or less) with shock Intervention: Late hydrocortisone with VIS >=10 Comparator: Inotrope alone Summary The guideline panel suggests that late hydrocortisone therapy as an adjunct to inotropes may not be used in the treatment of neonates with fluid refractory shock. (weak recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). This recommendation is to Diagnosis and Management of Shock in Neonates - National Neonatology Forum of India 58 of 111 be interpreted along with the recommendation for earlier use of hydrocortisone along with inotropes in neonates with fluid refractory shock. The use of late HC along with inotropes was adjudged to have significant side effects including mortality, NEC ≥ stage 2, fungal sepsis, hypertension, hyperglycemia requiring insulin therapy., increased duration of inotropes as well as hospital stay. Further, there were small desirable effects such as response to therapy and improved BP. Hence, the balance of effects favoured the comparator group of inotrope therapy alone. Though no studies had evaluated its cost effectiveness and the resources required, our judgement is that they may be not be favourable towards the intervention group of late HC along with inotropes. Similarly, the parameters of equity and values also favoured the comparator group of inotrope alone. All of the aforementioned parameters were considered before making this recommendation. The recommendation for earlier HC was also taken into account while making this recommendation. Among preterm neonates with transitional shock, which vasopressor or inotropic agent is preferred? Shock is common in preterm neonates during the initial days of postnatal life. [89] A sizeable proportion of these neonates are treated for isolated hypotension or hypotension with clinical features of hypoperfusion.[90] The most common causes of shock in preterm neonates are altered or unstable perinatal transition, septic shock, hypovolemic shock, and cardiogenic shock. In most scenarios, a volume bolus of 10-15 ml/kg is administered as a part of the initial management. [89][90][91] Fluid-refractory shock is treated with inotropes or vasopressors. Amongst the different types of shock, perinatal transitional instability is one of the most common causes of hypotension in the first few postnatal days of life especially in preterm neonates born at less than 28 weeks of gestation. The etiopathogenesis of transitional shock is multi-factorial and includes the failure of an immature myocardium to effectively respond to a sudden increase in the afterload immediately after birth (which occurs after the clamping of the umbilical cord), persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn secondary to conditions such as respiratory distress syndrome (RDS), and patent ductus arteriosus (PDA). [93][94][95] In many of the cases, transitional shock is accompanied by only low blood pressure (BP) values without any clinical or biochemical signs of hypoperfusion such as delayed capillary refilling time, decreased urine output, increasing levels of lactate etc.[91] Further, there exists no uniform definition for transitional circulatory instability. The other factor complicating the management of neonates with probable transitional circulatory instability presenting as isolated hypotension is that there is a paucity of evidence as to whether it should be treated at all.[19][39][95] While many studies have shown that treatment of isolated hypotension in the first few days of postnatal life may not translate to better clinical outcomes, some have shown an association between not treating severe isolated hypotension and poor short-term outcomes such as major brain injury (MBI) and NEC ≥ stage 2. [19][39]With the existence of such uncertainty in evidence, many clinicians treat isolated hypotension in this sub-group of preterm neonates. Adding to the conundrum is that different mean arterial (MAP) cut-offs are utilized to define hypotension. These include MAP less than GA, MAP < 30 mm Hg, and MAP < 3-10th centile based on GA, birth weight (BW) and postnatal age. [89][96][98] Some clinicians also take into account echocardiographic findings such as superior vena cava (SVC) flow, left ventricular output (LVO), right ventricular output (RVO), and maximum mean velocity in the pulmonary artery that are considered surrogate markers of perfusion to vital organs to guide treatment. [93][96][97][98] It is to be noted that alterations in these parameters have not been conclusively associated with poor cerebral perfusion. Dopamine is the most commonly used first-line inotrope to treat shock in preterm neonates. [99] However, many other inotropic agents and vasopressors such as dobutamine, epinephrine, milrinone, vasopressin, and hydrocortisone have also been evaluated in different studies. [79][100][101][103][91][102] To date, there exists no systematic review which had employed a network meta-analysis (NMA) in evaluating the efficacy of these medications in treating preterm neonates with probable transitional shock. Further, though many consider this state to exist until the first 24-48 hours of life, the timing of adequate transition to extrauterine life and hence the period of occurrence of transitional circulatory instability is a debated topic. The reasons that could be attributed to this could be the various effect modifiers such as antenatal corticosteroids, umbilical cord management, gestational age at birth, exogenous surfactant, and mechanical ventilation, all of which could affect the duration of the transition. [93][105][106][107][108] Considering these facts, we evaluated trials that included preterm neonates with shock (as defined by the authors) in the first week of postnatal life. If the inclusion criterion cut-off for postnatal age was not mentioned by the study authors, then the mean or median postnatal age was considered for inclusion. Most of the studies had included neonates of less than 24 hours of postnatal age. In this systematic review and NMA, our objective was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of various medications in the management of probable transitional circulatory instability. Since there exists no uniform definition for this condition, and there are other types of shock such as septic shock that may have a similar clinical presentation, there is a probability that some of the included neonates in our NMA may have had hypotension secondary to other causes as well. Those studies that have explicitly stated their patient population as neonates with septic shock or other types of shock such as secondary to necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) or hypovolemia were excluded. An NMA was chosen for data synthesis since multiple interventions were compared, and there is a paucity of head-to-head comparisons for most of these interventions. In such scenarios, an NMA allows for the provision of indirect evidence derived from the direct comparisons of randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Diagnosis and Management of Shock in Neonates - National Neonatology Forum of India 62 of 111 Practical info • While central lines remain the gold standard for continuous inotrope infusion due to the lower risk of extravasation injury, peripheral infusion under rigorous monitoring may be utilized in emergency situations. • Invasive blood pressure monitoring through an indwelling umbilical or peripheral arterial line may be considered in centers where facilities and skills for invasive monitoring are available. (refer to the recommendation on non-invasive versus invasive BP monitoring) • Blood sugars should be monitored at least 8 hourly and more frequently if hydrocortisone is also used as an adjunct. • Serial monitoring of lactate may not be a reliable marker for response to therapy when epinephrine is used to treat hypotension. • If a neonate with shock requires multiple inotropes, separate infusion pumps may be utilized. Y-connector can be used for connecting these infusions to the central venous access. • Increments and decrements of the infusion dosage should be done at 0.05 mcg/kg/min every 20 minutes to avoid rapid fluctuations in blood pressure which could result in major brain injury. Further, flushing of the epinephrine syringe to fill the dead space of the central line should be done before the insertion of the central line and should not be done after its insertion to avoid rapid fluctuations in blood pressure. • If echocardiography is available, serial monitoring of collapsibility of inferior vena cava and myocardial contractility along with other functional echocardiographic parameters could be considered during the course of treatment, provided expertise is available in interpreting the findings. • Health personnel should frequently monitor for equipment failure (eg. syringe pumps), central line blockage (eg. due to blood clots) and central line tip displacement • Anticipatorily reconstituted epinephrine infusion should be made ready before the infusion volume is about to get finished. • Terminal hub compatibility of other medications with epinephrine should be checked. • Strict aseptic precautions should be maintained while handling of the central line hubs. Evidence to decision Weak recommendation , Very low certainty evidence Epinephrine may be used as the first-line drug of choice in preterm neonates with fluid-refractory shock due to probable transitional circulatory instability in the first week of life. Epinephrine infusion may be started at a dose of 0.05 mcg/kg/min and incremented by 0.05 mcg/kg/min every 30 minutes till a maximum dose of 0.3 mcg/kg/min if the desirable endpoints are not achieved (Consensus statement). • This recommendation should be interpreted with the recommendations on permissive hypotension, volume of normal saline boluses, and adjuvant hydrocortisone therapy in preterm neonates. • This recommendation does not apply to neonates in whom hypovolemic, hemorrhagic or septic etiology of shock is suspected and where a relatively higher amount of volume expansion with crystalloids may be required before the initiation of inotropes or vasopressors. The recommendations for septic shock are provided separately (Consensus statement). However, based on the relative risk and 95% Credible Interval, it was adjudged that the balance of effects favored epinephrine as it possibly decreased the risk of the important outcomes of major brain injury (intraventricular hemorrhage > grade 2 and/or cystic periventricular leukomalacia) and necrotising enterocolitis ≥ stage 2. The important parameter of inconsistency could not be assessed and there was a probability of intransitivity related to some aspects. Considering all these, we made a weak recommendation. The other parameters of values, resource utilization, cost-effectiveness, equity, acceptability and feasibility were carefully evaluated, and most of these parameters were favourable towards epinephrine. The GDG is of the opinion that there is probably no uncertainty in how much the key stakeholders value the main outcomes. This is based on the expert consensus of the members of the working group. No substantial variability expected Values and preferences The GDG is of the consensus that the resources required would almost be the same for epinephrine and dopamine as all these medications are of similar cost and require similar equipment for instituting the intervention as well as for monitoring after the initiation of therapy. Vasopressin might require additional monitoring such as for hyponatremia, cardiac dysfunction due to increased afterload and end-organ ischemia. Hence, moderate savings of resources could be there if epinephrine is utilized instead of vasopressin. No important issues with the recommended alternative Resources Epinephrine possibly decreases both MBI and NEC ≥ stage 2. These severe complications require additional monitoring with serial ultrasonography of the brain for the progression of MBI and abdominal radiography for monitoring the response to treatment for NEC ≥ stage 2. Treatment with antibiotics / intravenous fluids / total parenteral nutrition for NEC ≥ stage 2 would also burden the healthcare system. Surgical interventions such as laparotomy for NEC stage 3 and shunt placement for progressive MBI may also be required in some neonates. Both complications prolong the duration of hospital stay as well. Finally, these adverse events are associated with poor long-term neurodevelopmental sequela adversely affecting the disability-adjusted life years (DALY). Hence, the GDG is of the consensus that, equity may be increased with the use of epinephrine as these valuable resources could be utilized for other sick neonates. Important issues, or potential issues not investigated Equity Epinephrine is a low-cost, frequently utilized medication in NICUs, and the clinicians are familiar with its adverse effects such as tachycardia, hyperglycemia, severe vasoconstriction at high dosages and increased lactate levels enabling them to monitor for these adverse effects. Hence, the GDG is of the consensus that epinephrine might probably be acceptable to the key stakeholders No important issues with the recommended alternative Acceptability Epinephrine is a drug which is of low cost and is readily available in all level 3 NICUs. Its institution and monitoring require the insertion of a central line, equipment such as multi-para monitors, point-of-care blood glucose monitors and arterial/venous blood gas analysis equipment that are usually available in level 3 NICUs. Hence, the GDG adjudged the feasibility aspect as "probably yes". Among neonates with cardiogenic shock due to perinatal asphyxia, which vasopressor or inotropic agent is preferred? Perinatal asphyxia is a common cause of myocardial dysfunction in neonates. [114] It has been shown that neonates with both hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) and cardiac dysfunction have poorer long-term neurological outcomes when compared to those with HIE alone. [115][116] A large proportion of neonates with moderate to severe hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) may require inotropic support. The efficacies of different inotropes in treating cardiogenic shock in neonates with perinatal asphyxia[117][118] have not been comprehensively evaluated. Hence, it is important that a systematic search of the literature be done, and a CPG be formulated guiding clinicians as to which inotrope may be the most efficacious in improving clinical outcomes in neonates with HIE and cardiac dysfunction. Two randomized controlled trials (RCTs) [119][120] and one observational study[121] have shown that prophylactic use of inotropes in neonates with perinatal asphyxia may not improve short-term outcomes. The observational study evaluated dobutamine and reported that the mean arterial pressure did not increase significantly with dobutamine administration. [121] Several studies have evaluated the trends in the pattern of mean arterial pressure and some echocardiographic indices in neonates with perinatal asphyxia and cardiac dysfunction. [122][123][124] Taiwo et al. reported that the mean arterial pressure in asphyxiated neonates is higher than in healthy neonates at birth. [122] While the MAP gradually increased in healthy term neonates, it showed a steady decrease in the first 6-12 hours of life in asphyxiated term neonates. Several studies have shown that asphyxiated neonates have impaired cerebral autoregulation and have correlated a higher superior vena cava (SVC) flow with poorer short - and long-term outcomes, irrespective of whether they were treated with therapeutic hypothermia or not. [123][124][125] This is quite contrary to the findings in preterm neonates where a higher SVC flow has been associated with better outcomes. [96] The other aspect that has been studied in asphyxiated neonates with cardiac dysfunction is the high prevalence of relative adrenal insufficiency (RAI).[126] Considering all these factors into account, it is imperative that the right choice of inotrope be utilized as the first line of management in asphyxiated neonates with cardiac dysfunction. Practical info Most studies had used a fluid bolus of normal saline prior to dopamine initiation. Hence, a single normal saline bolus of 10 ml/kg over half an hour may be used initially in neonates with cardiogenic shock secondary to perinatal asphyxia. • In units where echocardiography is available, the requirement of fluid bolus may be adjudged based on the inferior vena cava collapsibility. Further, other echocardiographic parameters may be monitored while the neonate is on dopamine therapy. • Other neuroprotective strategies such as maintaining euglycemia, avoiding hypocarbia/hypercarbia as well as hyponatremia and use of therapeutic hypothermia (if the neonate satisfies all the criteria for therapeutic hypothermia initiation) should be ensured. Evidence to decision Weak recommendation , Low certainty evidence There is insufficient evidence to recommend a specific vasopressor or inotropic agent as the first-line drug in neonates with cardiogenic shock secondary to birth asphyxia. Clinicians may choose to start dopamine, dobutamine, or epinephrine. Benefits and harms A total of 13 studies were included in the systematic review, of which 3 were synthesized in the meta-analysis. These two studies were underpowered resulting in a wide confidence interval.[127][129] Though the fixed effects model showed an improved response to therapy with dopamine, we chose the effect estimate from the random effects model as one study had studied neonates on therapeutic hypothermia, and the other did not use therapeutic hypothermia. Further, these two studies were done during different time epochs spanning almost 3 decades during which many aspects related to neonatal care have improved. Additional consideration for the desirable effects: The RCT by Kovacs et al. had initiated dopamine at 6 mcg/kg/min in both the groups (Dopamine with hydrocortisone vs. Dopamine alone) and incremented the dosage by 2 mcg/kg/min until 20 mcg/kg/min. Dopamine is most commonly utilized inotrope in asphyxiated neonates with cardiac dysfunction. [118] No study evaluating dobutamine or other inotropes was identified. However, prophylactic use of dobutamine was shown to have no effect on MAP in asphyxiated neonates in one observational study. [121] Also, dobutamine has been shown to increase the SVC flow in preterm neonates when compared to dopamine. [128] An increased SVC flow has been shown to be associated with poorer short- and long-term outcomes in asphyxiated neonates with cardiac dysfunction as described in the background section. With the paucity of evidence and the aforementioned effect of dobutamine on SVC flow, dopamine seems to be the preferential first-line inotrope in neonates with asphyxia and cardiac dysfunction. Undesirable effects Diagnosis and Management of Shock in Neonates - National Neonatology Forum of India 76 of 111 The RCT by Kovacs et al. reported that when dopamine was utilized alone, the undesirable effect of electrographic seizures was significantly lower when compared to dopamine along with hydrocortisone (Lower limit of 95% CI: 6 per 1000). [126] There were no differences between the two groups for the critical outcome of mortality. Also, there were no differences in the other outcomes of brain MRI abnormality, use of anticonvulsant therapy, acute kidney injury, sepsis, hyperglycemia or hypoglycemia, gastrointestinal bleeding, and duration of mechanical ventilation as well as hospital stay.[126] Montaldo et al. in their retrospective study of 64 infants who had undergone therapeutic hypothermia for HIE and were initiated on inotropes, reported that those neonates who were exposed to a dopamine dose of 5 mcg/kg/min (mean) (IQR: 0-5) and duration of 14 hours (12-15 hours) had a lesser risk of death or moderate to severe neurodevelopmental disability at 18-24 months of age. The same study reported that exposure to a dopamine dose of 7.5 mcg/kg/min (5 to 10) and duration of 28 hours (24-31 hours) was associated with a higher risk of death or moderate to severe neurodevelopmental outcomes. Similarly, the use of a dobutamine dose of 5 mcg/kg/min (IQR 5-8 mcg/kg/min) for a duration of 38 hours (30-41 hours) was associated with good long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes. A dobutamine dose of 10 mcg/kg/min (IQR: 7.5-10 mcg/kg/min) and for a duration of 61 hours ( IQR 56-67 hours) was associated with poor long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes at 18-24 months. Norepinephrine of any dosage or duration was associated with poorer long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes at 18-24 months of age. The same study by Montaldo et al. showed that neonates with a high SVC flow of 109 +/- 18 ml/kg/min were associated with higher odds of death or long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes compared to those with a low SVC flow of 78 +/- 19 ml/kg/min (adjusted odds ratio: 1.57 (1.1–1.78). [125] Pazandak et al. in their case-control study did not show any difference in the adverse outcomes of mortality, seizures, and brain MRI abnormality with dopamine exposure.[127] Balance of effects: The intervention evaluated is dopamine and the comparator is dopamine along with hydrocortisone. Though dopamine along with hydrocortisone was shown to be better for the outcome of the response to treatment in the RCT by Kovacs et al., the incidence of electrographic seizures was lower in the dopamine alone group.[62] Considering the importance of these two outcomes, the GDG is of the view that the balance of effects favors the dopamine-alone group. The meta-analysis of the two aforementioned observational studies showed a trend towards increased MAP with dopamine in neonates with asphyxia and cardiac dysfunction.[127][129] Additional considerations for the balance of effects: Kovacs et al. had shown a higher prevalence of RAI in neonates with perinatal asphyxia and HIE. [126] Also, Montaldo et al. had shown that exposure to higher doses and longer duration of dopamine was associated with poor long-term outcomes of death or moderate to severe neurodevelopmental disability. [125] Henceforth, we suggest initiating hydrocortisone with increasing dopamine requirement at a dose of ≥ 10 mcg/kg/min which is in line with the recommendation of use of hydrocortisone in shock by this GDG. This might not only improve the response to therapy but also may decrease the duration of inotrope requirement as described in the CPG on hydrocortisone use in neonates with shock. Subgroup considerations Of the studies included in the systematic review, all except one had used therapeutic hypothermia for treating moderate to severe hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy. Due to the unavailability of adequate data, sub-group analyses could not be performed. No important issues with the recommended alternative Feasibility Diagnosis and Management of Shock in Neonates - National Neonatology Forum of India 78 of 111 Rationale Dopamine is the most studied inotrope in neonates with cardiogenic shock secondary to perinatal asphyxia. Though hydrocortisone when initiated with dopamine at a dose of 5 mcg/kg/min improved the mean arterial pressure, it was associated with an increased risk of electrographic seizures. A low starting dose of 5 mcg/kg/min is suggested as one study had shown an association of higher dosage with long-term outcomes of mortality or moderate to severe neurodevelopmental disability. Two studies that evaluated prophylactic use of dopamine vs. dobutamine in neonates with perinatal asphyxia did not show any difference between the two groups. In line with the recommendation on the use of hydrocortisone, we suggested its use if the requirement of dopamine is ≥ 10 mcg/kg/min as hydrocortisone has been shown to improve the response to treatment and may shorten the duration of dopamine requirement. Longer duration of exposure to dopamine was also shown to be associated with poor long-term outcomes of mortality or moderate to severe neurodevelopmental disability in neonates with cardiogenic shock secondary to perinatal asphyxia. Further, one case-control study indicated that dopamine was safe in neonates with cardiogenic shock secondary to perinatal asphyxia and its exposure did not increase the risk of mortality, seizures, or brain abnormalities in MRI. We did not find any studies that evaluated epinephrine or milrinone in neonates with cardiogenic shock secondary to perinatal asphyxia. One study reported that dobutamine did not improve the mean arterial pressure in neonates with perinatal asphyxia. Also, a high superior vena cava (SVC) flow in neonates with cardiogenic shock secondary to perinatal asphyxia was shown to be associated with poor short- and long-term outcomes in two studies. Since dobutamine has been shown to increase SVC flow better when compared to dopamine and due to paucity of studies, we did not suggest dobutamine as the first line inotrope of choice in neonates with cardiogenic shock secondary to perinatal asphyxia. Implementation • Most studies had used a fluid bolus of normal saline prior to dopamine initiation. Hence, a single normal saline bolus of 10 ml/ kg over half an hour may be used initially in neonates with cardiogenic shock secondary to perinatal asphyxia. • In units where echocardiography is available, the requirement of fluid bolus may be adjudged based on the inferior vena cava collapsibility. Further, other echocardiographic parameters may be monitored while the neonate is on dopamine therapy. • Other neuroprotective strategies such as maintaining euglycemia, avoiding hypocarbia/hypercarbia as well as hyponatremia and use of therapeutic hypothermia (if the neonate satisfies all the criteria for therapeutic hypothermia initiation) should be ensured. Evaluation Data on short- and long-term outcomes with the use of dopamine as well as hydrocortisone in neonates with cardiogenic shock secondary to perinatal asphyxia is sparse. Hence, units that implement these recommendations should collect data prospectively on the same. Research needs • Apart from dopamine, no study has evaluated other inotropes such as epinephrine and milrinone in neonates with cardiogenic shock secondary to perinatal asphyxia and hence, it is a research priority. • There is a lacuna in literature comparing dopamine vs. dobutamine in neonates with perinatal asphyxia and cardiogenic shock. This is also a research priority. Among neonates with cardiogenic shock due to patent ductus arteriosus, which vasopressor or inotropic agent is preferred? The incidence of symptomatic patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) is high, especially in extremely low gestational age neonates. [132][133] Though the first line of management of a hemodynamically significant PDA is medical therapy, if the neonate does not respond to medical therapy, surgical intervention is indicated. During the course of therapy, the neonate can develop complications attributed to PDA such as oliguria, feed intolerance, necrotizing enterocolitis, intraventricular hemorrhage and shock. [134] Most of these complications are attributed to hypotension and the ensuing poor end organ perfusion. Henceforth, it is important that the literature be systematically reviewed and a CPG be formulated to guide the clinicians as to which inotropic or vasopressor agent is most efficacious in neonates with PDA with shock. The systematic review of the literature identified only two non-RCTs addressing this specific PICO. [130][131] Both the studies were of before-after design and had studied the effects of dopamine. Also, the outcomes evaluated in these studies were surrogate outcomes only. No study evaluating other inotropic agents or vasopressors were identified. Practical info • While one study had used a dosage of 5- 10 mcg/kg/minute (5) and had shown a good response to therapy, the GDG is of the consensus that a starting dose of 5 mcg/kg/min may be considered and titrated until 10 mcg/kg/min. • In some scenarios where higher doses are required, the clinician may increase the dopamine dosage in increments of 2 mcg/ kg/minute until a maximum dose of 20 mcg/kg/minute as used in the other study.(4) • Some of the aspects involved in implementing this recommendations are provided in other recommendations such as the use of volume expansion, monitoring of blood pressure, hydrocortisone therapy. Some other aspects are provided in the good practice statement section. Evidence to decision Weak recommendation , Very low certainty evidence • Dopamine may be used as the first-line inotrope in preterm neonates with shock secondary to hemodynamically significant patent ductus arteriosus. ◦ Dopamine may be initiated at a dosage of 5 mcg/kg/min and if needed incremented by 2 mcg/kg/min every 20 minutes until a maximum dose of 10 ug/kg/min. • There is insufficient evidence to recommend for or against other inotropic agents or vasopressors as the first-line drug. Desirable effects Meta-analyses of both the included studies indicated that dopamine may be effective in increasing systolic, diastolic, and mean blood pressures. Meta-analysis of the two studies also suggested that dopamine was associated with increased mean pulmonary arterial pressure, thereby decreasing the left to right shunting across the PDA. [130][131] While the time taken for the blood pressures to be normalized was 28 minutes (range 10 -60 minutes) in one study (dopamine dose used: 5-20 mcg/ kg/minute)[130], it was almost 120 minutes in the other study (5-10 mcg/kg/min)[131]. Both the studies had enrolled preterm neonates with a mean gestational age of approximately 28 weeks and a mean postnatal age of less than 5 days. Further, one study had reported improvement in other surrogate outcomes such as improved superior vena cava flow (by 30%), decreased mesenteric (0.95+/- 0.15 to 0.83+/- 0.17) and cerebral artery index (0.92 +/-0.20 to 0.77+/-0.18).[131] This observational study also reported that urine output increased from 1.9+/-1.2 to 2.9+/-1.4 mL/kg/hour (P < .05). A trend in decreased plasma lactate concentration was also reported by this study. Small net benefit, or little difference between alternatives Benefits and harms Diagnosis and Management of Shock in Neonates - National Neonatology Forum of India 83 of 111 Undesirable effects None of these studies had reported adverse clinical outcomes. One study reported an 8% (95% CI: 3%-13%; P <.05) increase in heart rate after the initiation of dopamine. [131]The authors of this study also reported that though the heart rate increased by 8%, the left ventricular output remained the same. Researchers evaluating the effect of various inotropic agents or vasopressors should evaluate critical and important outcomes such as mortality, severe grade intraventricular hemorrhage, necrotizing enterocolitis, retinopathy of prematurity requiring intervention, mortality, and long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes. Among neonates with septic shock, which vasopressor or inotropic agent is preferred? Volume expansion and inotropes or vasopressors are the mainstays of therapy in neonatal septic shock. Conventionally, dopamine is the most commonly used first-line vasoactive agent in neonatal septic shock.[135] Dopamine acts indirectly by releasing norepinephrine from presynaptic vesicles. However, there are concerns of the efficacy of dopamine in facilitating the release of norepinephrine, especially in preterm neonates with hypotension. [136] Epinephrine is emerging as a first-line vasoactive agent in the pediatric population. Adrenal insufficiency is also quite prevalent in neonates at the onset of shock. [137] Dobutamine or milrinone are primarily used if there are signs of myocardial dysfunction. However, in neonates with septic shock, vasoregulatory failure is the main pathophysiology of myocardial depression. [138] As of present, there are no existing guidelines on the management of neonatal shock, specifically about the question of the first-line vasopressor of choice. Henceforth, there is a need to systematically search the literature and derive evidence as to which is the most efficacious first-line vasopressor or inotropic agent in neonates with septic shock. Evidence to decision Weak recommendation , Low certainty evidence Dopamine or epinephrine may be used as the first-line vasoactive agent in neonates with septic shock. • Dopamine may be initiated at a dose of 10 mcg/kg/min and if needed incremented until a maximum dosage of 20 mcg/kg/ min. • Epinephrine may be initiated at a dose of 0.05 mcg/kg/min and if needed incremented every 20 minutes until a maximum dosage of 0.4 mcg/kg/min. Benefits and harms Desirable effects Only one RCT [139] was identified in the literature search (Figure 15). Small net benefit, or little difference between alternatives Benefits and harms Diagnosis and Management of Shock in Neonates - National Neonatology Forum of India 89 of 111 Figure 15: PRISMA flow of the literature search Data from this single RCT [139] with a small sample size reported that the dopamine and epinephrine groups were comparable for the outcomes of mortality, reversal of shock (by 45 minutes), and hemodynamic stability (no additional requirement of vasoactive agent by 2 hours). Subgroup analysis showed that in preterm neonates of less than 30 weeks of gestation (n=18), there was a statistically significant difference favoring the adrenaline group for the outcome of hemodynamic stability. Undesirable effects There was no statistically significant difference between dopamine and epinephrine for any undesirable effects as reported by this RCT. However, indirect evidence from a follow-up study of an RCT on preterm neonates with transitional shock had indicated that epinephrine may be associated with increased lactate levels requiring bicarbonate infusion (95% vs. 67%, p<0.05) and hyperglycemia requiring insulin infusion (45% vs 12%, p<0.05) when compared to dopamine. [110] Such findings were not observed in the RCT.[139] Balance of effects Considering the desirable and undesirable effects, the GDG is of the consensus that the balance of effects favors neither dopamine nor epinephrine. This judgment was based on the fact that though epinephrine resulted in better hemodynamic stability in preterm neonates of less than 30 weeks of gestation, the sample size was too small. On the other hand, the increased levels of lactate requiring bicarbonate infusion and hyperglycemia requiring insulin infusion were not reported by the RCT included in the formulation of this CPG. Further, these outcomes were neither critical nor important. ## Evaluation

Resuscitation should not delay while investigating the etiology of undifferentiated shock. Physicians should have a high clinical suspicion for the presence of shock, and an attempt to stratify the severity of the shock should also take place to assess the need for emergent or early interventions. Evaluation of undifferentiated shock should begin with a thorough history and physical examination.

Besides telemetry monitoring, a 12-lead electrocardiogram should be obtained. ECGs might show evidence of acute coronary syndrome, arrhythmias, or provide diagnostic clues suggestive of pericardial effusion or pulmonary embolism. [...] Laboratory tests in a patient with undifferentiated shock should include a CBC and differential, renal and liver function tests, serum lactate level, cardiac biomarkers, D-dimer level, coagulation profile, type and screen for a possible blood transfusion if appropriate (if concern for hemorrhagic shock), blood and urine cultures, and blood gas analysis. Initial imaging studies recommended in patients with undifferentiated shock and hypotension include chest x-rays to look for the source of infection such as pneumonia, complications of shock such as ARDS, clinical findings supporting the diagnosis of pulmonary edema in cardiogenic shock, widened mediastinum in aortic dissection. CT scans can also assist in unmasking the etiology of shock in appropriate clinical scenarios. Point of care [...] In a patient with undifferentiated shock, diagnostic clues to pericardial tamponade as the etiology include dyspnea, the Beck triad (elevated jugular venous pressure, muffled heart sounds, hypotension), pulses paradoxus, and known risk factors such as trauma, the recent history of pericardial effusion, and thoracic procedures.

Cardiogenic shock should be considered as the etiology if the patient with undifferentiated shock had chest pain suggestive of cardiac origin, narrow pulse pressure, elevated jugular venous pulsations or lung crackles, and significant arrhythmias on telemetry or EKG.

# Shock

Hayas Haseer Koya; Manju Paul.

#### Authors

#### Authors

Last Update: July 24, 2023.

## Continuing Education Activity

Shock is a life-threatening manifestation of circulatory failure. Circulatory shock leads to cellular and tissue hypoxia resulting in cellular death and dysfunction of vital organs. Effects of shock are reversible in the early stages and a delay in diagnosis and/or timely initiation of treatment can lead to irreversible changes including multiorgan failure (MOF) and death. This activity reviews the evaluation and management of shock, and explains the role of the interprofessional team in evaluating and treating patients with this condition.

**Objectives:**

[Access free multiple choice questions on this topic.](https://www.statpearls.com/account/trialuserreg/?articleid=28970&utm_source=pubmed&utm_campaign=reviews&utm_content=28970)

## Introduction

Shock is a life-threatening manifestation of circulatory failure.  Circulatory shock leads to cellular and tissue hypoxia resulting in cellular death and dysfunction of vital organs. Effects of shock are reversible in the early stages, and a delay in diagnosis and/or timely initiation of treatment can lead to irreversible changes, including multiorgan failure (MOF) and death.

## Etiology

Shock is characterized by decreased oxygen delivery and/or increased oxygen consumption or inadequate oxygen utilization leading to cellular and tissue hypoxia. It is a life-threatening condition of circulatory failure and most commonly manifested as hypotension (systolic blood pressure less than 90 mm Hg or MAP less than 65 mmHg). Shock is the final manifestation of a complex list of etiologies and could be fatal without timely management. There are mainly four broad categories of shock: distributive, hypovolemic, cardiogenic, and obstructive.[[1]](#article-28970.r1) The wide range of etiologies can contribute to each of these categories and are manifested by the final outcome of shock. Undifferentiated shock means that the diagnosis of shock has been made; however, the underlying etiology has not been uncovered.

**1. Distributive Shock**

Characterized by peripheral vasodilatation.

Types of distributive shock include:

**Septic Shock**

Sepsis is defined as life-threatening organ dysfunction resulting from dysregulated host response to infection.[[2]](#article-28970.r2) Septic shock is a subset of sepsis with severe circulatory, cellular, and metabolic abnormalities resulting in tissue hypoperfusion manifested as hypotension which requires vasopressor therapy and elevated lactate levels (more than 2 mmol/L)

The most common pathogens associated with sepsis and septic shock in the United States are gram-positive bacteria, including streptococcal pneumonia and Enterococcus.

**Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome**

Systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) is a clinical syndrome of the vigorous inflammatory response caused by either infectious or noninfectious causes. Infectious causes include pathogens such as gram-positive (most common) and gram-negative bacteria, fungi, viral infections (e.g., respiratory viruses), parasitic (e.g., malaria), rickettsial infections. Noninfectious causes of SIRS include but are not limited to pancreatitis, burns, fat embolism, air embolism, and amniotic fluid embolism

**Anaphylactic Shock**

Anaphylactic shock is a clinical syndrome of severe hypersensitivity reaction mediated by immunoglobulin E (Ig-E), resulting in cardiovascular collapse and respiratory distress due to bronchospasm. The immediate hypersensitivity reactions can occur within seconds to minutes after the presentation of the inciting antigen. Common allergens include drugs (e.g., antibiotics, NSAIDs), food, insect stings, and latex.

**Neurogenic Shock**

Neurogenic shock can occur in the setting of trauma to the spinal cord or the brain. The underlying mechanism is the disruption of the autonomic pathway resulting in decreased vascular resistance and changes in vagal tone.

**Endocrine Shock**

Due to underlying endocrine etiologies such as adrenal failure (Addisonian crisis) and myxedema.

**2. Hypovolemic Shock**

Hypovolemic shock is characterized by decreased intravascular volume and increased systemic venous assistance (compensatory the mechanism to maintain perfusion in the early stages of shock). In the later stages of shock due to progressive volume depletion, cardiac output also decreases and manifest as hypotension. Hypovolemic shock divides into two broad subtypes: hemorrhagic and non-hemorrhagic.

Common causes of hemorrhagic hypovolemic shock include

Common causes of non-hemorrhagic hypovolemic shock include:

**3. Cardiogenic Shock**

Due to intracardiac causes leading to decreased cardiac output and systemic hypoperfusion. Different subtypes of etiologies contributing to cardiogenic shock include:

**4. Obstructive Shock**

Mostly due to extracardiac causes leading to a decrease in the left ventricular cardiac output

## Epidemiology

Distributive shock is the most common type of shock, followed by hypovolemic and cardiogenic shock. Obstructive shock is relatively less common. The most common type of distributive shock is septic shock and has a mortality rate between 40 to 50%.

## Pathophysiology

Hypoxia at the cellular level causes a series of physiologic and biochemical changes, resulting in acidosis and a decrease in regional blood flow, which further worsens the tissue hypoxia.[[4]](#article-28970.r4) In hypovolemic, obstructive, and cardiogenic shock, there is a decrease in cardiac output and decreased oxygen transport. In distributive shock, there is decreased peripheral vascular resistance and abnormal oxygen extraction. Excitement is a spectrum of physiologic changes, ranging from early stages, which are reversible to the final stages, which are irreversible with multiorgan failure and death. Generally, shock has the following three stages:

## History and Physical

A focused history should be obtained from the patient (if feasible) and/or patient's relatives. Also, a review of the patient’s outpatient medical records (information regarding risk factors, medications, and trend of baseline vital signs including blood pressure), as well as hospital medical records, could give valuable clues regarding the patient's risk for shock and potential etiology. Clinical features and symptoms can vary according to the type and stage of shock. The most common clinical features/labs which are suggestive of shock include hypotension, tachycardia, tachypnea, obtundation or abnormal mental status, cold, clammy extremities, mottled skin, oliguria, metabolic acidosis, and hyperlactatemia.[[5]](#article-28970.r5)[[6]](#article-28970.r6) Also, features pertaining to the underlying cause of the shock can be present.

Patients with hypovolemic shock can have general features as mentioned above as well as evidence of orthostatic hypotension, pallor, flattened jugular venous pulsations, may have sequelae of chronic liver disease (in case of variceal bleeding).

Patients with septic shock may present with symptoms suggestive of the source of infection (example-skin manifestations of primary infection such as erysipelas, cellulitis, necrotizing soft-tissue infections), and cutaneous manifestations of infective endocarditis.

Patients with anaphylactic shock can have hypotension, flushing, urticaria, tachypnea, hoarseness of voice, oral and facial edema, hives, wheeze, inspiratory stridor, and history of exposure to common allergens such as medications or food items the patient is allergic to or insect stings.

Tension pneumothorax should be suspected in a patient with undifferentiated shock who has tachypnea, unilateral pleuritic chest pain, absent or diminished breath sounds, tracheal deviation to the normal side, distended neck veins and also has pertinent risk factors for tension pneumothorax such as recent trauma, mechanical ventilation, underlying cystic lung disease).

In a patient with undifferentiated shock, diagnostic clues to pericardial tamponade as the etiology include dyspnea, the Beck triad (elevated jugular venous pressure, muffled heart sounds, hypotension), pulses paradoxus, and known risk factors such as trauma, the recent history of pericardial effusion, and thoracic procedures.

Cardiogenic shock should be considered as the etiology if the patient with undifferentiated shock had chest pain suggestive of cardiac origin, narrow pulse pressure, elevated jugular venous pulsations or lung crackles, and significant arrhythmias on telemetry or EKG.

## Evaluation

Resuscitation should not delay while investigating the etiology of undifferentiated shock. Physicians should have a high clinical suspicion for the presence of shock, and an attempt to stratify the severity of the shock should also take place to assess the need for emergent or early interventions. Evaluation of undifferentiated shock should begin with a thorough history and physical examination.

Besides telemetry monitoring, a 12-lead electrocardiogram should be obtained. ECGs might show evidence of acute coronary syndrome, arrhythmias, or provide diagnostic clues suggestive of pericardial effusion or pulmonary embolism.

Laboratory tests in a patient with undifferentiated shock should include a CBC and differential, renal and liver function tests, serum lactate level, cardiac biomarkers, D-dimer level, coagulation profile, type and screen for a possible blood transfusion if appropriate (if concern for hemorrhagic shock), blood and urine cultures, and blood gas analysis. Initial imaging studies recommended in patients with undifferentiated shock and hypotension include chest x-rays to look for the source of infection such as pneumonia, complications of shock such as ARDS, clinical findings supporting the diagnosis of pulmonary edema in cardiogenic shock, widened mediastinum in aortic dissection. CT scans can also assist in unmasking the etiology of shock in appropriate clinical scenarios. Point of care ultrasonography or focused cardiac ultrasound is also a useful bedside diagnostic tool.[[7]](#article-28970.r7)

## Treatment / Management

The initial approach to management is the stabilization of the airway and breathing with oxygen and oral mechanical ventilation when needed. Peripheral IV or intraosseous infusion (IO) access should be obtained. Central venous access may be required in the setting of shock if there is difficulty securing peripheral venous access, or the patient needs prolonged vasopressor therapy or large-volume resuscitation. Immediate treatment with intravenous (IV) fluid should be initiated, followed by vasopressor therapy, if needed, to maintain tissue perfusion. Depending on the underlying etiology of shock, specific therapies might also be needed.

Septic shock - initial aggressive fluid resuscitation with IV isotonic crystalloids 30 mL/kg within 3 hrs with additional fluid based on frequent reassessment, empiric antibiotic therapy within one hr. [[8]](#article-28970.r8) For patients with septic shock requiring vasopressors, target a mean arterial pressure (MAP) of 65 mmHg. The first choice of a vasopressor is norepinephrine, with the addition of vasopressin if refractory.[[9]](#article-28970.r9)

Anaphylactic shock - aggressive IV fluid resuscitation with 4 to 6 L of IV crystalloids. Stop the offending agent, intramuscular epinephrine, antihistamines, corticosteroids, nebulized albuterol.

In adrenal crisis - judicious fluid resuscitation, IV dexamethasone.

Hypovolemic shock - obtain two large-bore IVs or central line. Place the patient in the Trendelenburg position. Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation with 2 to 4 L of isotonic crystalloids. PRBC transfusion if ongoing bleed. Appropriate medical or interventional strategies to treat the underlying etiology. Continue with isotonic crystalloids and use vasopressors if needed

Obstructive shock - the judicious use of IV crystalloids. If shock persists, early initiation of vasopressors-norepinephrine is the first choice and add vasopressin if refractory. Continue IV fluids but monitor very closely.

If acute massive pulmonary embolism -thrombolysis. Judicious use of IV fluids has a paradoxical worsening of hypotension; it may develop due to severe right ventricular dilatation and septal bowing compromising left ventricle filling.

If tension pneumothorax - needle thoracotomy followed by tube thoracotomy. If cardiac tamponade-pericardiocentesis, significant clinical improvement is possible, even with minimal fluid removal).

Cardiogenic shock - if unstable tachyarrhythmia or bradyarrhythmias, initiate ACLS protocol and cardioversion. Judicious use of IV fluids in the absence of pulmonary edema. Consider inotropes (dobutamine is the most commonly used agent) or intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP), if refractory shock, and vasopressor (norepinephrine) with inotropes.

If STEMI - consider thrombolysis or coronary revascularization procedures and or IABP.

## Differential Diagnosis

Uncovering the etiology of undifferentiated shock is very important. In a patient presenting with undifferentiated shock, the differential diagnosis includes a wide variety of etiologies that falls under the four major categories of shock, as outlined above. Also, sometimes patients can have a combination of shock syndromes. Another differential is "pharmacological shock," which results from vasodilatation or myocardial depression from medications (e.g., benzodiazepines, beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, opiates, anticholinergics, and sildenafil).

## Prognosis

Sepsis and septic shock, in general, are associated with long-term morbidity and mortality, with many of the survivors requiring placement into long-term acute care facilities or post-acute care centers.[[10]](#article-28970.r10)[[11]](#article-28970.r11) Septic shock has a mortality rate between 40% and 50%. Cardiogenic shock has a mortality rate ranging from 50% to 75%, an improvement over prior mortality rates. Hypovolemic and obstructive shock generally have much lower mortality and respond better to timely treatment.

## Pearls and Other Issues

## Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes

The management of patients with shock calls for a collaborative, interprofessional approach. Clinicians must react promptly to the emergency and determine the precise cause of shock. Nursing will be on hand to assist at every step of the way, assisting with measures such as intubation and administering medications. Pharmacists must rapidly prepare and deliver the needed drugs and yet still verify that dosing and interactions do not present a problem. Depending on the etiology, various specialists may also be called in on the case. Each area will need to act and react as the situation dictates. WIth interprofessional cooperation, these patients will stand a better chance of recovery from shock with minimal deleterious effects. [Level 5]

Does Point-of-Care Ultrasonography Improve Clinical Outcomes in Emergency Department Patients With Undifferentiated Hypotension? An International Randomized Controlled Trial From the SHoC-ED Investigators Paul R. Atkinson, MBBChBAO, MA*; James Milne, MD; Laura Diegelmann, MD; Hein Lamprecht, MBChB, PhD; Melanie Stander, MBBCh, MMed; David Lussier, MD; Chau Pham, MD, MBA; Ryan Henneberry, MD; Jacqueline M. Fraser, RNBN; Michael K. Howlett, MD, MHSA; Jayanand Mekwan, MBBS; Brian Ramrattan, MBBS; Joanna Middleton, MD; Daniel J. van Hoving, MBChB, MMed; Mandy Peach, MD; Luke Taylor, MD; Tara Dahn, MD; Sean Hurley, MD; Kayla MacSween; Luke R. Richardson, MD, MPH; George Stoica, PhD; Samuel Hunter; Paul A. Olszynski, MD, MEd; David A. Lewis, MBBS *Corresponding Author. E-mail: paul.atkinson@dal.ca, Twitter: @eccucourse.
Study objective: Point-of-care ultrasonography protocols are commonly used in the initial management of patients with undifferentiated hypotension in the emergency department (ED). There is little published evidence for any mortality beneﬁt. We compare the effect of a point-of-care ultrasonography protocol versus standard care without point-of-care ultrasonography for survival and clinical outcomes.
Methods: This international, multicenter, randomized controlled trial recruited from 6 centers in North America and South Africa and included selected hypotensive patients (systolic blood pressure <100 mm Hg or shock index >1) randomized to early point-of-care ultrasonography plus standard care versus standard care without point-of-care ultrasonography.
Diagnoses were recorded at 0 and 60 minutes. The primary outcome measure was survival to 30 days or hospital discharge. Secondary outcome measures included initial treatment and investigations, admissions, and length of stay.
Results: Follow-up was completed for 270 of 273 patients. The most common diagnosis in more than half the patients was occult sepsis. We found no important differences between groups for the primary outcome of survival (point-of-care ultrasonography group 104 of 136 patients versus standard care 102 of 134 patients; difference 0.35%; 95% binomial conﬁdence interval [CI] –10.2% to 11.0%), survival in North America (point-of-care ultrasonography group 76 of 89 patients versus standard care 72 of 88 patients; difference 3.6%; CI –8.1% to 15.3%), and survival in South Africa (point-of-care ultrasonography group 28 of 47 patients versus standard care 30 of 46 patients; difference 5.6%; CI –15.2% to 26.0%). There were no important differences in rates of computed tomography (CT) scanning, inotrope or intravenous ﬂuid use, and ICU or total length of stay.
Conclusion: To our knowledge, this is the ﬁrst randomized controlled trial to compare point-of-care ultrasonography to standard care without point-of-care ultrasonography in undifferentiated hypotensive ED patients. We did not ﬁnd any beneﬁts for survival, length of stay, rates of CTscanning, inotrope use, or ﬂuid administration. The addition of a point-of-care ultrasonography protocol to standard care may not translate into a survival beneﬁt in this group.
